title: Meta’s New Gen 3 Smart Glasses Are Mostly Familiar
gist: WIRED rates Meta's Gen 3 Nova smart glasses ($299) 7/10: lighter, better-looking, with nine-hour battery and a stronger six-mic array, but largely iterative over Gen 2, with a still-poor AI assistant and ongoing privacy/creep concerns around camera glasses.

insights.claim: Meta's Gen 3 smart glasses bring no revolutionary upgrades: battery rises to nine hours (one more than Gen 2), the 12-MP 3K-video cameras are unchanged, and the improved mic array matches the Meta Glasses that debuted in June.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Product cadence is iterative, suggesting a maturing category competing on style and price rather than capability.
insights.quote: none of the upgrades in Meta’s new Gen 3 glasses are revolutionary
insights.locator: In fact, none of the upgrades

insights.claim: The six-mic system strongly suppresses background noise on calls; in testing, a blaring fire alarm was inaudible to the caller.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Call quality is a credible everyday use case beyond AI and camera.

insights.claim: Meta's own-brand Nova glasses cost $299, while Ray-Ban-branded Gen 3 models start at $499, and Nova offers dozens of frame/color combinations with a smaller camera housing that colleagues didn't notice.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Meta is building a lower-priced own brand alongside EssilorLuxottica partner brands, broadening the price ladder.
insights.quote: The Ray-Ban-branded Gen 3 models are more expensive, starting at $499.
insights.locator: The pair of glasses I’ve been using

themes.theme: AI assistant remains the weak link

insights.claim: Meta's current on-glasses AI assistant is 'still terrible', failing even to describe the glasses' own features when shown the product page.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: AI, the strategic justification for smart glasses, is not yet delivering, a risk to Meta's AI-wearables narrative.
insights.quote: Unfortunately, Meta’s current AI assistant on the glasses is still terrible.

insights.claim: Meta's Muse AI is coming to the glasses later this year; the reviewer finds Muse more useful than the current assistant but notes it seems better at surveilling than helping users.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Muse integration is the next catalyst for the glasses' value proposition, with privacy baggage attached.
insights.quote: a service that seems better at surveilling than helping its users

insights.claim: Conversation Focus, an accessibility mode for hard-of-hearing users, is in early access only on Ray-Ban and Oakley models, not Meta's own-designed frames.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Feature segmentation across brands; accessibility could be a differentiating use case.
insights.locator: They feel and function the same

insights.claim: Camera-equipped Meta glasses have become prime targets of controversy for use by creeps and abusers; Meta has made the recording indicator light more tamper-proof and launched camera-free audio-only glasses.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Social/regulatory backlash is a real adoption headwind; Meta is hedging with camera-free SKUs.
insights.quote: That’s not necessarily enough to deter the creeps.
insights.locator: If you pretty much ignore the AI
